title: Perfect Squares
description: Brute force to optimized: uncached recursion trying every square combination versus a bottom-up dp table reusing smaller-value answers.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer n, return the fewest number of perfect square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, and so on) that sum exactly to n.

blocks.text: Find the smallest number of perfect squares (each at least 1) that add up to exactly n.

blocks.title: Analogy: Making Change With the Fewest Coins, Where Coin Values Are Perfect Squares
blocks.text: Picture making change for an amount n using coins whose values are exactly the perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, ...), and needing the fewest coins possible. Just like coin change, the fewest-coins answer for a given amount can be built from the fewest-coins answers of smaller amounts.

blocks.caption: The answer for i is 1 plus the best answer for i minus some perfect square

blocks.text: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, three perfect squares, the fewest possible.

Before exploring every possible combination of squares recursively from scratch, notice that the answer for a given n only depends on the answers for smaller values, values that get recomputed over and over across different combinations.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the first square chosen is j squared, the remaining problem is exactly "fewest squares summing to n minus j squared," a smaller version of the same problem.

Observation 2: Trying every valid j squared at most n, and taking the best result plus 1, gives the answer for n.

Observation 3: Many different choices of the first square, across many different top-level values of n, end up asking about the SAME smaller remaining value, redundant work if not cached.

Observation 4: Building a table of answers from 0 up to n, in order, ensures every smaller answer is already available (computed once) when it is needed for a larger one.
This leads to a bottom-up dynamic programming table, where dp[i] is built from previously computed dp values at i minus each valid perfect square.
Recursively try every valid perfect square as the first pick, and recurse on the remainder, without caching any results.

items: For a given remaining amount, try every perfect square j squared that is at most that amount.
Recursively solve for the remainder after subtracting that square, and add 1 to the result.
Take the minimum over every choice of square.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recursively try every square, re-solving overlapping subproblems repeatedly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every call re-explores every possible square choice from scratch, with no memory of previously solved remainders.
The same remainder value can be reached through many different combinations of earlier square choices, each triggering a fresh, identical computation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, since overlapping subproblems are recomputed repeatedly without caching.
Space: O(square root of n) for the recursion depth.
Limitation: the same remaining amount is solved over and over across different branches of the recursion tree, wasting enormous effort that a simple lookup table would avoid entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing is wasteful: many different sequences of square choices lead back to the exact same remaining amount, and each one re-derives the same answer independently.

What to cache: the fewest-squares answer for every amount from 0 up to n, built once and reused whenever needed.

How to build it in order: since dp[i] only depends on dp values at STRICTLY SMALLER indices (i minus a positive square), computing dp from 0 upward guarantees every value dp[i] needs is already finished.

The core idea: build a table dp[0..n], where dp[i] is 1 plus the best dp value among i minus every perfect square at most i, computed once per value.

Build an array dp of size n plus 1, with dp[0] equal to 0. For each i from 1 to n, try every perfect square j squared at most i, and set dp[i] to the minimum of 1 plus dp[i minus j squared] over all such j. Return dp[n].

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the dp table once, from smaller values upward

blocks.text: Since dp[i] only depends on dp values at strictly smaller indices, building the table from 0 upward guarantees every value it needs is already finished. Each dp[i] is computed exactly once, by trying every perfect square that could have been the last one added, and reusing the already-solved answer for what remained before it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times square root of n), for every i, trying every square up to it.
Space: O(n) for the dp table.

blocks.text: Perfect Squares is a direct application of the coin-change dynamic programming pattern, where the "coin values" happen to be perfect squares; the fewest-squares answer for any amount only depends on fewest-squares answers for smaller amounts.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "this looks like a classic problem", think: it is Coin Change, with perfect squares as the coin denominations.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in exponential time; the optimized dynamic programming approach runs in O(n times square root of n) time and O(n) space.

items: Pattern: bottom-up dynamic programming, the same pattern as Coin Change, with perfect squares as denominations.
Core Idea: dp[i] is 1 plus the best dp value among i minus every perfect square at most i, built once from smaller values upward.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n times square root of n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(square root of n) for the brute force's recursion, O(n) for the optimized dp table.
Most Important Observation: this is Coin Change with perfect squares as the coin values, and shares its overlapping-subproblem structure.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once recognized as a coin-change variant.
One line memory trick: coin change, coins are perfect squares.
